items.title: gobench: a tool for comparing Go benchmark runs across branches
items.author: Alex Chan
items.content:
I’ve recently joined a new team that’s focused on performance, stability, and scalability – a change from my previous projects, where traffic was low enough that performance was rarely a concern.

This codebase has already gone through multiple rounds of optimisation, so there’s no low-hanging fruit left. Any proposed change is inherently complex, and it’s rarely obvious whether a tweak will actually speed things up or slow them down. To measure the impact of our work, we’re leaning on the benchmarking tools in Go’s standard library.

On one of my recent pull requests, I wrote a benchmark, and I pasted the output from two before/after runs. Paul improved this with a short shell script that ran multiple samples, and compared the results with the benchstat command.

N..6C613000cfc12d4cecho$N:$Cgitcheckout-q$C./tool/gotest-run^X-benchBenchmarkPostureAnalyzer./control/posture/analysis/tee-abench-$C.txtbenchstatbench-fc12d4c.txtbench-613000c.txt

benchstat does statistical analysis on the output from multiple runs, which is more reliable and easier to read than the raw output. In particular, it puts all the data in a single table, and shows the percentage change against the baseline.

I like this script, but it’s a little fiddly. I have to identify the two commits to compare, it leaves text files in my working directory, and it leaves my repo in a detached head state when it’s done. I wanted something more ergonomic.

I’ve written a new tool gobench to give me a smoother experience. I check out my feature branch, run gobench with the arguments I’d pass to , and it prints the final analysis from benchstat.

Under the hood, it creates a Git work tree for the base branch (leaving my working directory as-is), captures the benchmark output in memory (so there are no extra text files), and does an alternating sample of benchmarks.

The alternating samples is a feature I really like from Paul’s original script. I run benchmarks on my laptop rather than a dedicated workstation, and the benchmarks could be sensitive to thermal throttling, background processes, or other things happening on my computer. Alternating between the two branches reduces the effect of this noise.

Let’s look at an example. Suppose my main branch has a recursive implementation of Fibonacci numbers, while my feature branch has an iterative approach. Unsurprisingly, the iterative approach is faster, and gobench makes it easy to quantify the improvement.

gorun./cmd/gobench./example/fib/-benchBenchmarkFib

My first version of gobench was an expansion of Paul’s script, but as I started adding features, it became clear that Bash was the wrong tool. I rewrote it as a Go tool that shells out to , , and .

If you’d like to try gobench yourself, the code is available in my gotools repository, or you can install it with:

goinstallalexwlchan.net/gotools/cmd/gobench@latest

gobench has already saved me from shipping code that looked fast on paper but regressed in practice. As I keep working on performance-critical Go code, having low-friction benchmarks will make it easier to test my ideas early and often.

items.title: Verifying my web archives with Playwright
items.author: Alex Chan
items.content:
To protect against link rot and disappearing content, I save local copies of web pages I like into my web archive.

Ideally, this archive is completely self-contained. I want a local copy of each page’s HTML and all the assets it depends on (CSS, images, scripts, and so on). I don’t want my archived pages fetching resources from the original website, which could disappear at any time.

Initially, I was verifying self-containedness by hand. I’d open each saved page in a web browser, and check the browser dev tools. I’d check the Console tab for errors and failed requests, and watch the Network tab for requests going out to the internet. That approach was tedious and error-prone, and I wanted something better.

I now automate the process using Playwright, a testing framework that allows you to control web browsers. I open each page using Playwright, and check if it’s making external requests.

Detecting external requests in Playwright

When you open a page in Playwright, you can subscribe to events which tell you when the page issues a request.

In this Python snippet, we start Playwright, start a WebKit browser, and open a new page. We tell the page to append external requests to a list, and then load . We see that makes two requests on page load: one for , and one for a JavaScript file.


    sync_playwright
    closingpwebkitlaunch
    closingbrowsernew_page
    pageon msg requestsappendmsg

    pagegoto

print requests

In a more complex scenario, we might use Playwright to interact with the page after loading – for example, clicking a button or filling in a form, and then we could see the requests triggered by each action.

Once we have a list of requests made by the page, we can inspect the property to check if any of them were fetching from an external website. I wrote a function to carry out this check:

 Request str bool requrl  original_url urllibparseurlsplitoriginal_url urllibparseurlsplitrequrl org_urlscheme  req_urlscheme  org_urlnetloc  req_urlnetloc req_urlscheme

assert_page_is_self_contained(ctx, url)

I’ve wrapped these two steps in a function assert_page_is_self_contained(ctx, url), which is part of my chives utility library.

The function takes a Playwright (or ) and a URL, then:

  1. Opens a new page in the browser
  2. Loads the URL in the page
  3. Checks what happened when the page completes loading

It throws an exception if there are any:

  • Uncaught page exceptions or errors
  • Console warnings or errors
  • Requests targeting external resources

The function tries to trigger important network requests that might be skipped on the initial page load. For example, it evaluates the body’s to force a synchronous reflow, which causes the browser to request any lazily loaded images or fonts that might otherwise be missed.

Here’s an example which verifies a file from the working directory:


    sync_playwright
    closingpwebkitlaunch
    assert_page_is_self_containedbrowser urlfile_uri

I originally passed a as the first argument, but changing the function to take a or lets it manage its own pages. It gets a fresh page for every verification, and closes it when it’s done. (The first time I ran this, I created a new page for every verification, and never closed them – my computer ground to a crawl as my script opened hundreds of browser tabs.)

If you create a new context, you can emulate different browser settings, like location, locale, and window size. Here’s an example where we use contexts to test the same page in light/dark mode:


    sync_playwright
    closingpwebkitlaunch closingbrowsernew_contextcolor_scheme
        assert_page_is_self_containedlight_ctx urlfile_uri closingbrowsernew_contextcolor_scheme
        assert_page_is_self_containeddark_ctx urlfile_uri

In my web archive, I check every page in light/dark mode, and at 1×/2× pixel densities. It takes at least a second to run each verification, so I cache the results. As I save new pages, they’re added to a verification queue, and I’m warned of any missing assets.

Unsurprisingly, the first run flagged many missing fonts and images, which I added to my local archive. Every saved page now passes cleanly.

Browser is best-effort, but may still miss things

Even with automated testing, it’s difficult to guarantee a completely self-contained archive. Different instances of a browser might load different assets, and a single page load might miss different variations:

  • Responsive images – web pages can offer different sizes of an image, and the browser chooses a specific size based on the current window dimensions
  • Appearance settings – a browser might load different fonts or images depending on light/dark mode
  • Interaction-dependent assets – a web page might have assets that are only required on hover or user action

You can mitigate some of this by testing with multiple contexts or adding post-load interactions, but every step makes the process take longer. Fortunately, most of the pages I save are simple, blog-style pages where I’ve stripped out the JavaScript. For my specific use case, initial load verification is more than good enough.

There are other projects where it could be useful to intercept and audit the requests made by a web page:

  • Verifying your Content Security Policy (CSP). The CSP header restricts what resources can be loaded by a web page, and you could check that your configuration has the correct effect.
  • Auditing login screens. You could check that sensitive pages don’t load any external scripts, which mitigates the risk of credential theft via a compromised third-party.
  • Testing analytics and tracking. You could script user flows, like a shopping cart checkout, and confirm that tracking events fire correctly.

I don’t do much front-end web development, but Playwright has become a key tool in my toolbox. I read a lot about people using AI agents and MCPs to interact with websites, but I prefer Playwright. It’s more fiddly and requires explicit instructions, but it’s constrained, deterministic, and I never have to worry about it doing something unexpected.
